title: The Model diagram, redrawn
subject: How a unit, its pattern, parts and frame codes, and the code behind them relate, for a reader new to the codebook

brief.background: The Map's Browser tab now opens on Model, meant to introduce the UI codebook's concepts before the tabs that examine them. Its first diagram, seven boxes joined by verbs with a cardinality at each end, asks the reader to learn that notation before the concepts and shows no screen, and the owner judged it unclear. The questions raised along the way show what the reader needs: whether a unit is a whole screen or something smaller, how a pattern differs from a unit, whether a pattern can sit inside part of a unit, and where the Alpine component fits. An earlier board, UI concepts, drawn (2026-11-01), sketched eight ways to relate the same concepts; its pick became a Layers tab, later dropped.
brief.methodology: Every sketch draws the same real unit, the Map's Docs tab, simplified: a list as its pattern, frame codes including tabs, a search box, count chips and a filter rail, and map.js as the code that draws it. Each concept must let a reader new to the codebook say what a unit, a pattern, a part and a frame code are, and where markup and code fit, or else say which of those it leaves out. Colors follow the unit shots, amber for frame codes and blue for the pattern, with violet for parts and slate for the unit and its code. The eight differ in mechanism or form, not styling.

ideas.title: The outlined shot
ideas.kind: borrowed form: the census's own unit shot
ideas.commentary:
The census already shoots every coded unit with its frame codes outlined in amber and its main region in dashed blue, each labelled with its code's name. One real shot, shown large beside a key, introduces unit, frame code and pattern on pixels the reader has seen, at no drawing cost.

It shows neither parts nor code, and on a busy tab the outlines crowd the content they label.

ideas.title: Build it up
ideas.commentary:
Four frames of the same tab, each adding one concept: the screen as a unit, its main region as a pattern, that region's pieces as parts, the controls around it as frame codes; a last step names the code that draws it. Each term is placed on the screen before the next arrives, in the order a reader looks.

It costs room: four frames where the other ideas use one.

ideas.title: One kind, many screens
ideas.commentary:
A pattern card above three different units whose main regions it describes. It answers the question this session raised directly: a unit is one screen, and a pattern is a kind of layout that many screens share.

Frame codes and code are left out, so it explains two concepts well rather than all of them.

ideas.title: Swap the pattern
ideas.commentary:
The Docs tab twice, with the same controls and the same documents, once as a list and once as a card grid. Changing only the main region's layout isolates what a pattern is: the arrangement, as distinct from the content and the controls.

It says nothing about parts, code or markup, and the card-grid twin is invented.

ideas.title: Zoom in
ideas.kind: mechanism: scale, down to a pattern inside a part
ideas.commentary:
Closer and closer frames: the Map view, its Docs tab as a unit, the list region as its pattern, then one item as a part, holding a smaller pattern of its own. It answers whether a pattern can appear inside part of a unit, and places the unit inside the view that hosts it.

A view is not one of the codebook's terms, so the first step may blur where a unit begins.

ideas.commentary:
One row per concept in three columns: what the reader sees, the codebook's name with its value on the Docs tab, and how the markup or the census records it. A compact reference that holds every concept, the markers and the Alpine component included.

It explains by mapping, so it assumes the reader already has the screen in mind.

ideas.title: One sentence
ideas.commentary:
One sentence describes the Docs tab, each concept's words in its color: a unit whose main region is a list of items, chosen by tabs, a search box and chips, drawn by map.js. A reader meets the terms by their role in a description they can check against the tab.

It rests on one example, and color alone carries the mapping.

ideas.title: Questions first
ideas.kind: information structure: the reader's questions as the index
ideas.commentary:
Six questions a reader would ask of any screen, each answered by a term and its value on the Docs tab. The questions do the defining, so the terms arrive as answers rather than as vocabulary.

Without a picture it relies on the reader having the tab open.

grafts: each step captioned by the question it answers
a closing step showing the list pattern in two other units
the parts step ending on a pattern held inside one item
selection.rationale: The relational diagram asked the reader to learn its notation before its concepts, and showed no screen. Building up one real tab introduces one term at a time on something the reader recognizes, in the order a reader looks: the screen, its main region, that region's pieces, the controls around it, then the code. The questions make each step's purpose plain, the closing specimens settle how a pattern differs from a unit, and the nested item answers whether a pattern can sit inside part of a unit.
assumptions: Is the Docs tab the right specimen, or would a tab with fewer frame codes read faster?
Is a drawn wireframe clear enough, or should each step mark up the real shot?
Do the Alpine component and kits belong on this tab, or only a pointer to the Kits tab?
On a phone, do five stacked frames read as a sequence, or does the tab need a step control?
